title: New data released on Obama administration's "accidentally collected" information on Americans during election
text: Newly released data describe information about Americans that was "accidentally collected" by the National Security Agency. A lawyer for the American Civil Liberties Union said of the information accidentally collected: "I think it is alarming. There seems to be a universal trend toward more surveillance and more surveillance that impacts Americans privacy without obtaining a warrant." During his final year in office, President Barack Obama's team significantly expanded efforts to search National Security Agency intercepts for information about Americans. The team distributed thousands of intelligence reports across government containing the unredacted names of U.S. residents during the divisive 2016 presidential election. Obama's top aides routinely made use of rules that the president had relaxed starting in 2011 to help the government fight terrorism, espionage by foreign enemies and hacking threats. Dozens of times in 2016, those intelligence reports identified Americans who were directly intercepted talking to foreign sources or who were the subject of conversations between two or more monitored foreign figures. The data, made available this week by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, provide the clearest evidence to date of how information about Americans accidentally collected by the NSA overseas was subsequently searched and disseminated. This took place after President Obama loosened privacy protections in 2011 to make such sharing easier in the name of national security. A court affirmed his order. The information is particularly sensitive because the NSA is legally forbidden from directly spying on Americans, and its authority to conduct warrantless searches on foreigners is up for renewal in Congress later this year. The release also comes as lawmakers investigate President Trump's own claims that his privacy was violated by his predecessor during the 2016 election.

title: Kevin McCarthy, next in line for Speaker of the House, withdraws from race
text: Rep. Kevin McCarthy (R-CA) has withdrawn from the race for House Speaker. The reason he gave the Republican Caucus for withdrawing was: "I am not the right person to lead at this moment." McCarthy had been expected to win the Speakership by a wide margin, but his comments on Benghazi were viewed unfavourably by his fellow Republicans. His statement that the Benghazi investigation was all about politics was exactly what Hillary Clinton needed to revive her campaign. Ultimately, he was concerned that he could not secure the 218 votes needed to win. McCarthy's decision, announced moments before Republicans were set to nominate their candidate, will postpone the vote for speaker. Before withdrawing, McCarthy had been running against Reps. Jason Chaffetz, R-Utah, and Daniel Webster, R-Fla., and it is unclear whether other candidates will now come forward. Although McCarthy, R-Calif., faced vocal opposition from some conservative members and groups, he was thought to have more than enough support to win the party's nomination in the vote initially scheduled for Thursday. In announcing his choice, McCarthy told colleagues that it was not his time. His withdrawal unsettled fellow lawmakers, particularly his allies in the leadership. Speaking to reporters afterward, McCarthy said he thinks the party needs a fresh face.

title: Still shut! Maria leaves Buckeye's Puerto Rico oil terminal crippled
text: Days after Hurricane Maria tore through the Caribbean, leaving a trail of destruction and at least 25 people dead, Buckeye Partners LP's Yabucoa oil terminal in Puerto Rico was still shut on Friday, the company said. And the damage? Nobody is saying. The U.S. oil storage and transportation company would not say whether the tanks at the 4.6-million-barrel terminal were hit by the monster storm, which slammed ashore near Yabucoa. All it would say is that a full assessment of the facility is under way. "We are working to maintain the safety and well-being of our Yabucoa, Puerto Rico employees," it said in a statement. Buckeye is not alone. A bigger terminal run by U.S. firm NuStar Energy LP on the island of St. Eustatius, able to store up to 13.03 million barrels of oil, has also been stuck, unable to reopen after an earlier hurricane, Irma, damaged several tanks. The fallout is serious. Closed oil terminals across the Caribbean and restrictions on loading and unloading large vessels at several Texas ports have choked flows of crude and refined products across the Atlantic in recent weeks. And Maria is not finished! The second major hurricane to batter the Caribbean this month lashed the Turks and Caicos Islands on Friday, after knocking out power to all of Puerto Rico and driving several rivers to record flood levels.

title: Melanesian tribe's DNA carries genes from unknown species, confirming lost children of the Anunnaki
text: Scientists have discovered that islanders from Melanesia possess genes belonging to an unknown hominid species, a finding that raises the question of whether it proves the Anunnaki ancestry of humans. On October 20, the American Society of Human Genetics held its annual meeting, and the conclusions reached there were described as staggering. The data gathered show that people from Melanesia, an area in the South Pacific that includes Papua New Guinea and its neighbouring islands, may carry unusual genes in their DNA. The geneticists believe the unrecognized DNA belongs to a previously undiscovered species of humanoids. According to Ryan Bohlender, one of the researchers involved in the study, that species is not Neanderthal or Denisovan but something entirely different. "We’re missing a population or we’re misunderstanding something about the relationships," he said. The Denisovans are an extinct species belonging to the hominid genus. They were named after the Denisova Cave in the Siberian Altai Mountains, where the first bone fragment belonging to the species was found. Very little is known about this related species. "Human history is a lot more complicated than we thought it was," Bohlender said. The statement is accurate. Humanity's complex past is being brought to light step by step, and discoveries such as this one point in one direction: humans may not be who they think they are. The study includes the following passage: "With assumptions about population size and more recent population separation dates taken from the literature, we estimate the archaic-modern separation date at ~440,000 ± 300 years ago for all modern human populations."

title: 'He must step down!' Furious crowds turn on Zuma as ANC succession war erupts
text: The streets were full of fury. Thousands of South Africans marched in anti-corruption protests on Wednesday, a rallying cry against scandal-soaked President Jacob Zuma and his powerful allies, just three months before a new ANC leader is chosen. The stakes could hardly be higher. The African National Congress will pick its next leader in December, with Deputy President Cyril Ramaphosa expected to face off against Nkosazana Dlamini-Zuma, the former chair of the African Union and Zuma's ex-wife. The Congress of South African Trade Unions (COSATU), which has backed Ramaphosa and operates in an alliance with the ANC, led the marches in major cities across the country. Anti-corruption? That was the official line. But it quickly became obvious that protesters had come to vent their anger at Zuma and throw their weight behind his rivals. Throngs of protesters marched on parliament in Cape Town, singing and waving "Zuma must go" placards, though the crowds never came close to the tens of thousands COSATU had promised. Textile worker Florence Titus did not hold back: "Things are just going down under President Zuma. He needs to play a president's role not just be there to fill his pockets and his family's pockets. He must step down." She is not alone. Senior ANC figures have also demanded that Zuma quit in recent months, after a wave of allegations that his friends, the Gupta family, wield undue influence over the award of state contracts worth hundreds of millions of dollars. The Guptas and Zuma deny wrongdoing and claim they are victims of a politically-motivated witchhunt. Zuma survived a bid in parliament to force him from office in August, but he limped away politically wounded after some ANC members backed the opposition's no-confidence motion.

title: Obama administration's EPA proposes tougher mileage standards for trucks
text: The EPA continues to seek further restrictions on emissions. The Obama agenda is continuing and has been strengthened by the Pope's call for action on global warming, which is a scam. The agenda is political and has nothing to do with the truth about climate, and this is evident to any reasonable observer. The Obama administration on Friday proposed tougher mileage standards for medium and heavy-duty trucks, the latest step by President Barack Obama in his second-term effort to reduce pollution blamed for global warming. The Environmental Protection Agency issued new rules that would lower carbon dioxide emissions from trucks and vans by 24 percent by 2027. The rules would cut fuel costs by about $170 billion and reduce oil consumption by up to 1.8 billion barrels over the lifetime of vehicles sold under them. The long-expected rules were issued one day after Pope Francis released a teaching document calling on the world to take action to slow climate change. "With emission reductions weighing in at 1 billion tons, this proposal will save consumers, businesses and truck owners money," McCarthy said. "At the same time, the rules will spur technology innovation and job-growth, while protecting Americans health and our environment over the long haul," she said.

title: Look, but don't touch! The West Village 'public' garden you're locked out of
text: A fragrant mound of rose bushes, thyme beds, and magnolia and crab apple trees rises from an old roadway reclaimed as open space. There is just one problem. It is not open at all! It sits behind a locked gate in the heart of the West Village. No benches. No visiting hours. It is called the Sheridan Square Viewing Garden, and, just as the name says, you can only look. "It’s pretty, but there’s almost no point," said Alec Haley, a New York University student who walks past it every day. "Parks are supposed to be enjoyed and not just stared at." How did this happen? Long before New York City's plazas and parks were packed with lunchtime crowds savouring lattes and kale salads, the city launched a campaign to carve small pockets of greenery out of dormant or unused stretches of roadway to break up the streetscape. Back then, the city was a far more dangerous place. Some of these open spaces had to be locked up or scrapped over fears they would become magnets for loiterers, criminals and homeless people. In Herald Square, a bustling pedestrian plaza now sits just steps from Macy's, yet store officials fought hard to stop it being built in the 1980s, according to a former city transportation official. That official, Samuel I. Schwartz, the traffic commissioner from 1982 to 1986, said that in those days even chairs were nailed down so they would not be stolen. Of spaces like the viewing garden, he said: "They were closed to people, open to your eyes." The Sheridan Square Viewing Garden, planted in 1982, was one of the most striking of these street experiments. And it is hardly the only public garden that keeps the public out.

title: Obama can appoint a Supreme Court justice before he leaves office; it is unclear whether he will
text: President Obama, who has disregarded the US Constitution and has no respect for the rule of law, has the ability to appoint a Supreme Court Justice before he leaves the White House. It is not known whether he will do so. For a brief period the Senate will go into what is known as an intersession recess, creating a single opportunity for the president to test his recess-appointment powers by sending Judge Garland to the high court. A small number of activists have asked him to attempt it, but Mr. Obama has given no indication that he is considering it. The White House did not respond to a request for comment. The move would be a legal gamble under the high court's last ruling on recess appointments, in 2014. That 9-0 decision overturned several of Mr. Obama's early 2012 appointments, finding that the Senate was in session when the president acted and that he therefore could not use his powers. The ruling also stated, however, that there is a difference between appointments made during the annual yearlong session of Congress, known as intrasession, which Mr. Obama used in 2012, and appointments made at the end of the year after Congress adjourns, known as intersession. William G. Ross, a law professor at Samford University in Birmingham, Alabama, said Mr. Obama would have the power to elevate Judge Garland. He said, however, that it would be politically unwise and would damage the prestige of the court. The consensus is that Mr. Obama would be making a mistake to test that theory. "I think it’s fair to use the word stretch. I don’t know why he would try this."

title: Privacy be damned! House intel panel rams through NSA spying bill
text: Privacy advocates are furious. On Friday a U.S. House panel approved legislation that would renew the National Security Agency's warrantless internet surveillance program, brushing aside fierce objections from the technology sector and civil liberties groups over woefully inadequate privacy protection. The House Intelligence Committee voted 13-8 to reauthorize Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act for another four years, until 2021. Without congressional action, the act expires on Dec. 31. But do not expect a quick fix. The vote showed just how far Congress remains from any consensus on renewing Section 702, with several rival bills carrying various new privacy provisions circulating in the House and Senate, and no clear path forward for any of them. Intelligence agencies insist Section 702 is vital to national security and to protecting American allies, and the Trump administration wants barely any changes to it. Privacy advocates blasted the panel's bill for failing to require a warrant to access collected data belonging to Americans. Reform Government Surveillance, a group representing tech giants including Facebook, Alphabet's Google and Apple that pushes governments around the world to strengthen digital privacy protections, issued a lengthy statement on Thursday slamming the measure, which it warned may expand government surveillance. The vote split cleanly along party lines. Every Republican on the panel backed the measure, while every Democrat opposed it over a mix of concerns, including language that would change how officials can "unmask" the identity of Americans' names typically redacted in intelligence intercepts. Republicans, including President Donald Trump, have accused, without evidence, the previous administration of President Barack Obama, a Democrat, of improperly unmasking names for political reasons, a charge Democrats have rejected. And the scale is staggering: Section 702 lets the NSA scoop up vast amounts of digital communications from foreign suspects living outside the United States.

title: Europe pushes back! Allies demand Trump spell out his Middle East peace plan
text: America's closest allies are losing patience. On Friday, Britain, France, Germany, Sweden and Italy called on the United States to put forward detailed proposals for peace between Israel and the Palestinians, and branded President Donald Trump's decision to recognize Jerusalem as Israel's capital unhelpful. The fallout was swift and bloody. Trump's reversal of decades of U.S. policy on Wednesday sparked a Palestinian day of rage on Friday. Thousands of Palestinians took to the streets, scores were hurt and at least one was killed in clashes with Israeli troops. With fury sweeping the Arab world and alarm growing among Washington's Western allies, the United Nations Security Council met on Friday at the request of eight of its 15 members: Britain, France, Sweden, Bolivia, Uruguay, Italy, Senegal and Egypt. In a joint statement after the meeting, Britain, France, Germany, Sweden and Italy said the U.S. decision, which includes plans to move the U.S. embassy to Jerusalem from Tel Aviv, was unhelpful for prospects of peace in the region. "We stand ready to contribute to all credible efforts to restart the peace process, on the basis of internationally agreed parameters, leading to a two-State solution," they said. "We encourage the U.S. Administration to now bring forward detailed proposals for an Israel-Palestinian settlement." Egypt's U.N. Ambassador Amr Aboulatta went further, warning that the U.S. decision would have a grave, negative impact on the peace process. And Washington's response? Defiance. U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley insisted that Washington has credibility as a mediator with both Israel and the Palestinians, and accused the United Nations of damaging rather than advancing peace prospects with unfair attacks on Israel. "Israel will never be, and should never be, bullied into an agreement by the United Nations, or by any collection of countries that have proven their disregard for Israel’s security," Haley said.
